welcome.transcript: Welcome — and thank you for opening Beijing Echo, your personal audio guide to China's capital. Here's how it works. With your permission, this page uses your location on your device to find nearby places in the guide. As you explore, stories can play automatically when you come within range of a listed stop — imperial palaces, ancient temples, hutong alleys, and the Great Wall itself — like a local friend walking beside you. When a usable heading is available, a story can begin by telling you which way to look. Without it, we skip that direction cue. Street too noisy to hear every word? Tap Show transcript to expand the English text and read at your own pace. No accounts, no fees, no sign-up — just walk. Keep this page open and your screen on, and allow location access; playback also depends on your signal and browser. Now — head toward anything that looks interesting. Enjoy Beijing.

spots.name: Tiananmen Square
spots.summary: You are standing on Tiananmen Square — one of the largest public…
spots.transcript: You are standing on Tiananmen Square — one of the largest public squares on Earth, covering about four hundred and forty thousand square meters. For centuries this was the front courtyard of the imperial city, closed to ordinary people. Today it belongs to everyone. To the north rises the Gate of Heavenly Peace, from which Mao Zedong proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 — his portrait still hangs there today. Around you: the Great Hall of the People on the west, the National Museum of China on the east, the Monument to the People's Heroes at the center, and the Mausoleum of Mao Zedong to the south. Every sunrise, crowds gather for the flag-raising ceremony, timed to the moment the sun breaks the horizon. Walk north toward the gate, and behind it waits the Forbidden City — the next chapter of your walk.

images.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Gate of Heavenly Peace

spots.name: The Forbidden City (Palace Museum)
spots.summary: You've just stepped into the Forbidden City — a vast imperial palace…
spots.transcript: You've just stepped into the Forbidden City — a vast imperial palace complex, and for nearly five hundred years, a place where access was strictly controlled. Built by the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty and completed in 1420, it was home to twenty-four emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties. Its old name says it all: the Purple Forbidden City — a palace set apart from the city around it. Behind its walls: thousands of rooms in halls and courtyards, with gardens and a central north-south axis that runs through the heart of Beijing. Since 1987 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Palace Museum inside holds over a million treasures. Walk up the central axis: the Hall of Supreme Harmony — the throne hall used for enthronements and major state ceremonies — is one of the palace's grandest sights. Give it at least two hours. You'll only see a fraction.

images.credit: Photo: Pixelflake, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Hall of Supreme Harmony

spots.name: Jingshan Park
spots.summary: You're entering Jingshan Park — and it holds the single best view…
spots.transcript: You're entering Jingshan Park — and it holds the single best view in Beijing. This hill right in front of you is man-made: five peaks of soil dug out to create the moats of the Forbidden City directly to the south. Climb to the pavilion on top, turn around, and you'll see it — the entire Forbidden City, its golden roofs stretching to the horizon, laid out like a stage set. It also holds a tragic story. In 1644, as rebels stormed the city, the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, fled into this park and hanged himself from a tree — and with him, the Ming dynasty ended. The tree standing today is a descendant of the original, marked with a plaque. Come at sunset if you can: first the panorama, then the drums of the city at dusk. Jingshan is where Beijing reveals its perfect geometry.

images.credit: Photo: Charlie fong冯成, Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Wanchun Pavilion at the hilltop

spots.name: Beihai Park
spots.summary: Welcome to Beihai Park — one of the oldest imperial gardens in…
spots.transcript: Welcome to Beihai Park — one of the oldest imperial gardens in China, over a thousand years in the making. Right in front of you, across the water, rises its icon: the White Dagoba, a Tibetan-style stupa built in 1651 by the first Qing emperor to honor a visit by the Dalai Lama. The lake itself — Beihai means "Northern Sea" — was the playground of emperors for centuries: they boated in summer and skated across the ice in winter. This garden perfected a Chinese art: recreating an entire imaginary world in miniature — islands as immortal mountains, water as the sea. Look for the Nine-Dragon Wall near the north shore, one of the finest glazed-brick walls in China, its nine dragons each a different color. locals come here at dawn to dance, sing opera, and practice calligraphy with water brushes on the stone paths. Join the morning; it's magical.

images.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the White Dagoba on Jade Flower Island

spots.name: Shichahai Lakes
spots.summary: You've arrived at Shichahai — three linked lakes that have been the…
spots.transcript: You've arrived at Shichahai — three linked lakes that have been the soul of old Beijing for seven hundred years. The name means "ten temple lake", for the ten Buddhist and Taoist temples that once lined these shores. This is where the Grand Canal once ended: in the Yuan dynasty, barges unloaded silk and grain right here, making this the busiest harbor of the empire's capital. Today the lakes are Beijing's favorite escape — willow-lined shores, hutong lanes, and in winter, locals skating across the frozen water on traditional ice sledges. Cross the little arched Yinding Bridge — the "Silver Ingot Bridge" — one of the most photographed corners of the city, where old men fish in the morning and young people gather at dusk. All around you, the hutong neighborhoods that grew up around the lakes are among the best preserved in Beijing. Slow down here. This is the Beijing people fall in love with.

images.credit: Photo: Kyla Duhamel, CC BY 2.0 · via Flickr

landmark.name: the Yinding Bridge, the Silver Ingot Bridge

spots.name: Nanluoguxiang
spots.summary: This is Nanluoguxiang — an eight-hundred-year-old hutong from the Yuan dynasty, and…
spots.transcript: This is Nanluoguxiang — an eight-hundred-year-old hutong from the Yuan dynasty, and one of the oldest alleys still standing in Beijing. Its name means "South Luogu Alley", and its layout is remarkable: the main alley runs about eight hundred meters north to south, with sixteen side hutongs branching out like the legs of a centipede — locals have called it "the Centipede Street" for centuries. This chessboard plan dates to the founding of Yuan-dynasty Dadu, the city that became modern Beijing. What makes it special is the mix: gray-brick courtyard homes — siheyuan — standing beside cafés, bakeries, and design shops. Each side hutong hides its own stories: former residences of generals, painters, and playwrights are marked with plaques as you wander. Go at a quiet hour if you can, and step into the side alleys — that's where the eight hundred years actually live.

images.credit: Photo: Anagoria, CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the south entrance gate of Nanluoguxiang

spots.name: Yonghe Temple (Lama Temple)
spots.summary: You've reached the Yonghe Temple — Beijing's most vibrant Tibetan Buddhist temple,…
spots.transcript: You've reached the Yonghe Temple — Beijing's most vibrant Tibetan Buddhist temple, still thick with incense smoke and prayer. Its story begins as a royal residence: built in 1694 for the prince who would become the Yongzheng Emperor. When he took the throne, the palace could no longer be a home — so in 1744 it was converted into a monastery of the Gelug school, the "Yellow Hat" tradition of Tibetan Buddhism. That's why it looks like a palace: golden roofs and red walls, Han Chinese and Tibetan styles fused into one. Inside, don't miss the Guinness-record giant: an eighteen-meter statue of the Maitreya Buddha, carved from a single sandalwood trunk — it took three years to transport the log to Beijing. Come early, breathe the sandalwood air, and spin a prayer wheel as you go — locals will show you how.

images.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Hall of Harmony and Peace

spots.name: Imperial College & Confucius Temple
spots.summary: You're walking along Chengxian Street — Beijing's only surviving ancient board-and-plate paved…
spots.transcript: You're walking along Chengxian Street — Beijing's only surviving ancient board-and-plate paved lane — toward two treasures sharing one wall: the Confucius Temple and the Imperial College, the Guozijian. On your way in, pass under the Archway of Superior Learning — one of the only wooden archways in Beijing not painted in imperial yellow. The Confucius Temple, founded in 1302, honors China's great teacher: look for the nearly two hundred stone steles engraved with the names of more than fifty thousand scholars who passed the imperial examinations over five centuries — the largest honor roll you'll ever see. Beside it, the Imperial College was the empire's highest school, where the sons of nobility studied for those very exams. At its center stands the Biyong, a square hall on an island of water, where the emperor himself lectured — the "hall of learning surrounded by a moat". Ancient cypresses, some over seven hundred years old, shade it all.

images.credit: Photo: Philip Larson, CC BY-SA 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Biyong Hall

spots.name: Temple of Heaven
spots.summary: You've just stepped into the Temple of Heaven — and for five…
spots.transcript: You've just stepped into the Temple of Heaven — and for five hundred years, this is where China's emperors came to speak with the sky itself. Twice a year, the Ming and Qing emperors left the Forbidden City in solemn procession and traveled here to pray for good harvests — for the empire, this was the most important ritual of the year. At the heart of the complex rises the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests: a circular masterpiece of wood, famous for being built without a single nail, standing on three tiers of marble. The circle stood for heaven; the square grounds below, for earth. When UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1998, it called the temple "a masterpiece of architecture and landscape design" that shaped the Far East for centuries. But here's the secret locals know: this is also a park. On weekend mornings, thousands gather — dancing, singing opera, playing chess under ancient cypresses. Stay a while. Heaven can wait.

images.credit: Photo: Shujianyang, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests

spots.name: Qianmen & Dashilan
spots.summary: You've arrived at Qianmen — "the Front Gate" — the grand southern…
spots.transcript: You've arrived at Qianmen — "the Front Gate" — the grand southern gateway of old Beijing, and just beyond it, Dashilan, the city's oldest shopping street, six hundred years in the making. When the Qing court banned night life inside the imperial city, merchants, theaters, and teahouses all crowded here instead — and Dashilan became the entertainment capital of old Peking: the cradle of Peking opera, home to the city's first cinemas. The old brands are still trading: Tongrentang, the pharmacy of imperial physicians since the seventeen century; Zhangyiyuan tea; Neiliansheng, the cloth-shoe maker whose slippers once suited Qing officials. Look down as you walk — the street's name comes from the big wooden gates that once closed it at night. And look up at the Zhengyangmen archery tower behind you: part of the medieval city wall that once ringed all of Beijing. Duck into the side alleys — the old theater courtyards still echo.

images.credit: Photo: © Vyacheslav Argenberg, VascoPlanet.com, CC BY 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Zhengyangmen Archery Tower

spots.name: The Summer Palace
spots.summary: Welcome to the Summer Palace — the greatest imperial garden that survives…
spots.transcript: Welcome to the Summer Palace — the greatest imperial garden that survives on Earth, and Beijing's masterpiece of water and hills. Covering nearly three square kilometers — three-quarters of it water — this was the summer retreat of the Qing court, who fled the heat of the Forbidden City for the breezes of Kunming Lake. Everything here is deliberate: the lake was expanded by hand, and the earth dug from it was piled into Longevity Hill before you. Walk the Long Corridor — seven hundred meters of painted walkway, its beams holding thousands of classical scenes — said to be the longest painted corridor in the world. At its end, the Marble Boat waits: a stone vessel where the Empress Dowager Cixi famously lounged — paid for, critics said, with money meant for the imperial navy. And the story ended as critics warned. Come at golden hour, rent a boat, and see what emperors saw.

images.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Tower of Buddhist Incense on Longevity Hill

spots.name: Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan)
spots.summary: You're entering the Old Summer Palace — Yuanmingyuan, the "Garden of Gardens"…
spots.transcript: You're entering the Old Summer Palace — Yuanmingyuan, the "Garden of Gardens" — and its evocative ruins. In the eighteenth century this developed into a vast imperial garden complex: halls, pavilions, and libraries spread across three hundred and fifty hectares of hills and lakes, housing art and treasure. Emperor Qianlong even commissioned a section of European palaces — baroque fountains and marble facades designed by Jesuit court artists — whose remains can be seen in the Western Mansions area. Then, in October 1860, Anglo-French forces looted and burned the palace during the Second Opium War. The ruins are preserved as a reminder of that destruction, and the park is a place to reflect on this chapter of history. Walk slowly. This place is not about what stands — it's about what was lost, and what a garden once meant.

images.credit: Photo: 颐园新居, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Great Fountain ruins, Dashuifa

spots.name: 798 Art Zone
spots.summary: Welcome to 798 — where a cold-war electronics factory became China's contemporary…
spots.transcript: Welcome to 798 — where a cold-war electronics factory became China's contemporary art capital. These vast halls were built in the nineteen fifties with East German assistance, in genuine Bauhaus style: look up at the sawtooth roofs, angled north so uniform, soft light would pour into the workshops — a factory designed like a photographer's studio. The plant made military electronics for decades, then fell silent. In the early two-thousands, starving artists discovered what collectors now pay fortunes for: those chimneys, pipes, and red propaganda slogans painted on factory walls became the raw aesthetic of Chinese contemporary art. Galleries moved in, then museums, then the world — today 798 hosts hundreds of galleries and design shops, and its exhibitions range from ink painting to digital art. No ticket needed to wander. Grab a coffee in a former workshop, and let the factory walls surprise you — this is where today's China argues with its own history, in paint and steel.

images.credit: Photo: Cory M. Grenier, CC BY-SA 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the main factory gallery with Bauhaus sawtooth roofs

spots.name: Wangfujing
spots.summary: You've stepped onto Wangfujing — Beijing's most famous shopping street, seven hundred…
spots.transcript: You've stepped onto Wangfujing — Beijing's most famous shopping street, seven hundred years of commerce in motion. Its name means "Wang Family Well" — for the ten wells that once served this district when it was home to princes and their mansions in the Ming and Qing dynasties. When modern China opened up, this became the first great shopping boulevard of Beijing — and today it's a mile of department stores, century-old food brands, and neon, entirely pedestrianized in its southern stretch. This is the place to taste Beijing fast: the food halls nearby serve everything from roast duck to candied hawthorn skewers — tanghulu — and the brave queue for the snack street's more adventurous offerings. For a quieter contrast, slip into St. Joseph's Church at the street's east side — a baroque-style church from sixteen fifty-five, still holding mass amid the shopping crowds. Seven centuries in one street — go hungry, and go slow.

images.credit: Photo: Hal 0005, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Wangfujing pedestrian street clock tower

spots.name: Badaling Great Wall
spots.summary: This is it — the Great Wall of China, at Badaling, its…
spots.transcript: This is it — the Great Wall of China, at Badaling, its most famous gateway. The wall beneath your hands is not one wall but many, built and rebuilt across two thousand years; the brick wall you're standing on dates to the Ming dynasty, the fifteen to sixteen hundreds, when Beijing was the capital it guarded. The old saying goes: "He who has never been to the Great Wall is not a true man" — 不到长城非好汉 — and Badaling is where emperors, presidents, and millions of travelers have earned that title. Watch how it behaves like a living creature: it rides the spine of the mountains, its towers placed within sight of each other — smoke signals once leapt from tower to tower, carrying news of invasion to the capital at astonishing speed. Badaling was the first section opened to visitors, in the nineteen fifties, and it's fully restored and ramped for every age. Climb to the highest tower you can — the wall disappears into the mountains both ways. That view is the China postcard, and you're standing in it.

images.credit: Photo: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the highest watchtower of the Badaling section

spots.name: Mutianyu Great Wall
spots.summary: You've chosen the connoisseur's Great Wall: Mutianyu. Same Ming-dynasty wall, same mountain-spine…
spots.transcript: You've chosen the connoisseur's Great Wall: Mutianyu. Same Ming-dynasty wall, same mountain-spine engineering — but wrapped in forest instead of the city crowds. This section guarded the northeast approach to Beijing for centuries, and its builders showed personality here: it boasts more watchtowers than most sections, including a rare pair of towers built as one triple-height giant, and the crenellations come in both rectangular and sawtooth patterns — a detail found almost nowhere else. For centuries this wall slept under vines and pines; restoration in the nineteen eighties reopened it, and today a cable car lifts you up, and — if your inner child insists — a toboggan slide brings you down. Walk east toward tower twenty-three and you'll feel what most visitors never do: silence, wind, and the wall stretching on beyond sight. Come in October, and the mountains burn red with maple and smoke-tree leaves. This is the Great Wall at its most beautiful.

images.credit: Photo: Velatrix, CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the watchtower cluster at Mutianyu ridge

spots.name: Ming Tombs (Sacred Way)
spots.summary: You've arrived at the Ming Tombs — the valley where thirteen emperors…
spots.transcript: You've arrived at the Ming Tombs — the valley where thirteen emperors of the Ming dynasty sleep beneath the mountains. The site was chosen by feng shui masters: mountains arc around it like dragon wings, and a river winds through — an emperor's paradise. Every visitor walks the Sacred Way first: a several-kilometer avenue lined with colossal stone statues — two rows of creatures, from camels and elephants to mythical qilin and xiezhi, each carved from single blocks five centuries ago. They stand guard in pairs: one kneeling, one standing — so that even a tired spirit guard never sleeps on duty. At the end, the archway and the dragon-phoenix gates frame your approach to the tomb valleys. Only one tomb has ever been opened: Dingling, the Underground Palace, excavated in the nineteen fifties — step down into the vaulted chamber of stone and stand where the Wanli Emperor was laid to rest with his two empresses. The mountains hold the rest — thirteen emperors, one valley, five hundred years of silence.

images.credit: Photo: Charlie fong, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Sacred Way stone animal statues

spots.name: Prince Gong Mansion
spots.summary: You've entered Prince Gong's Mansion — the most complete princely residence surviving…
spots.transcript: You've entered Prince Gong's Mansion — the most complete princely residence surviving in Beijing, and the most dramatic biography of any house in the city. It began as the estate of Heshen, the most corrupt — and richest — official of the Qing empire: his private fortune, the story goes, exceeded the imperial treasury itself. When the emperor's son took the throne, Heshen was forced to take his own life, and the mansion passed to Prince Gong — its name ever since. Walk the front halls, then slip through to the surprise behind: a vast private garden of rockeries, ponds, and pavilions — including a Western-style gate, rare for its time — and a hidden stone that legend ties to imperial misfortune. Don't miss the courtyard opera house — all-wood acoustics, no nails in its hollow frames — where performances still play today. One mansion, two dynasties, one spectacular downfall. Beijing history, condensed into a single walled garden.

images.credit: Photo: onion83, CC BY-SA 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the opera house courtyard of Prince Gong Mansion

spots.name: Drum Tower & Bell Tower
spots.summary: These two towering gray buildings — the Drum Tower and the Bell…
spots.transcript: These two towering gray buildings — the Drum Tower and the Bell Tower — were once the clock of Beijing. For centuries, city life moved to their sound: at dusk the great drums beat, at dawn the great bell rang — twenty-five booming strikes marking the opening and closing of the city gates. Inside the Drum Tower you can still see the original timekeeping instruments: the water clock that measured the hours for centuries, and ranks of great drums — the largest, a single hide over two meters across. The towers date to the Yuan dynasty — the older you look, the more impressive that is — and both were rebuilt under Ming and Qing emperors. Climb the steep stairs — they were built for duty, not comfort — and you'll stand where the night watch once stood, holding the whole city in one glance: hutongs breaking like waves around lakes to the south. In this neighborhood, time still moves slowly. These towers are the reason.

images.credit: Photo: Toadspike, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Drum Tower's great timekeeping drums

spots.name: Houhai
spots.summary: This is Houhai — "the Back Sea" — where old Beijing comes…
spots.transcript: This is Houhai — "the Back Sea" — where old Beijing comes out to play at night. One of the Shichahai lakes, Houhai spent centuries as an aristocratic playground: princes built their gardens here, opera barges floated on summer nights. Today the tradition continues in modern costume: the south and east shores glow with lantern-lit bars and live music venues, while just one hutong back, families play chess under the willows as if the neon didn't exist. That contrast is the magic of Houhai — and your evening plan writes itself. At dusk, walk the shore from the Yinding Bridge: swans and pedal boats at golden hour, then music rising as the lights come on. In winter the lake freezes solid and becomes Beijing's great ice playground — sledges, skates, and sixty-year-old hockey games. Come for a drink, stay for the people-watching — Houhai is where Beijing's daytime shyness ends.

images.credit: Photo: chinogypsie, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the lakeside bar street of Houhai's south shore

spots.name: Liulichang Cultural Street
spots.summary: You've slipped into Liulichang — the quietest famous street in Beijing, and…
spots.transcript: You've slipped into Liulichang — the quietest famous street in Beijing, and its most literate. For five hundred years this has been the haunt of scholars: in Qing dynasty times, examination candidates flooded the city and lodged nearby, and booksellers, calligraphers, and antique dealers set up shop here to feed the hungry minds. The name means "Colored Glaze Factory", from the Ming dynasty kilns that once fired imperial roof tiles on this very ground. Today it's a street of art: brushes ground by hand, ink stones, rubbings, seals carved while you wait, and silk-mounted paintings. Its crown jewel is Rongbaozhai — the "Studio of Glorious Treasures" — a three-hundred-year-old workshop where artists still produce woodblock prints using techniques passed down for generations; each print may take months and dozens of carvings. Come early, watch a seal-cutter work, and leave with a brush made the old way. This is Beijing's slow, scholarly soul — hiding in plain sight.

images.credit: Photo: Shazari, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the archway at the east entrance of Liulichang

spots.name: Panjiayuan Antique Market
spots.summary: Welcome to Panjiayuan — Beijing's greatest treasure hunt, and the largest antique…
spots.transcript: Welcome to Panjiayuan — Beijing's greatest treasure hunt, and the largest antique and crafts market of its kind in China. What began as a spontaneous "dirt market" — vendors spreading their wares on the ground before dawn — is now a city block of thousands of stalls: Mao-era memorabilia, porcelain, jade, seals, faded family photos, Buddhist statues, lamps, lacquer, and things no category can hold. The unwritten rule: much of what you'll see is old-styled rather than old — so browse for beauty, bargain with humor, and never buy what you can't afford to love as a replica. The market's soul is the weekend: vendors arrive before sunrise, and serious hunters come with flashlights. Prices start high and drop with a smile and a walk-away — halving the first quote is normal. Bring cash-sized patience and small bills, keep your valuables front, and give yourself two hours. Everything here has a story — and half the fun is the vendor telling it.

images.credit: Photo: Steven Sun, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the main gate arch of Panjiayuan Market

spots.name: Beijing Ancient Observatory
spots.summary: You've found one of the most unlikely survivals in Beijing: a working…
spots.transcript: You've found one of the most unlikely survivals in Beijing: a working astronomical observatory from the Ming dynasty, standing beside the second ring road since fourteen forty-two. For nearly five hundred years, astronomers climbed this platform nightly to track the heavens for the emperor — because in imperial China, the sky was politics: eclipses and comets were omens, and the calendar was the throne's business. The bronze instruments on the roof are the stars of the show — armillary spheres, sextants, and a celestial globe, cast in the late sixteen hundreds under the direction of Ferdinand Verbiest, a Flemish Jesuit priest who served the Kangxi Emperor as court astronomer. Look closely: European engineering wrapped in Chinese dragons and clouds — East and West collaborating three centuries before "globalization". Few visitors find this place; those who do, climb a medieval tower and touch the instruments that once mapped the sky for an empire. Astronomy, diplomacy, and survival — all in one rooftop.

images.credit: Photo: User:Vmenkov, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the bronze instruments atop the observatory platform

spots.name: Olympic Green (Bird's Nest & Water Cube)
spots.summary: Welcome to Olympic Green — Beijing's monument to its two Olympic Games,…
spots.transcript: Welcome to Olympic Green — Beijing's monument to its two Olympic Games, two thousand eight and two thousand twenty-two — the only city on Earth to host both the Summer and Winter editions. Before you rises the Bird's Nest — the National Stadium — its tangled steel lattice designed by architects Herzog & de Meuron with artist Ai Weiwei as consultant. It cost years of engineering to make randomness look effortless: every beam is placed, none is decor. Beside it, the glowing blue cube is the Water Cube — the National Aquatics Center, where swimming world records famously fell like dominoes in two thousand eight — and which was later transformed, astonishingly, into the "Ice Cube" curling venue for the Winter Games. At night the whole park lights up — the nest glows red, the cube shimmers blue, and families fly kites on the great axis between them. Come after sunset: this is Beijing's modern skyline of dreams, and it photographs best in the dark.

images.credit: Photo: Picrazy2, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Bird's Nest National Stadium

spots.name: Fragrant Hills Park (Xiangshan)
spots.summary: You've arrived at Fragrant Hills — the Beijing autumn that everyone talks…
spots.transcript: You've arrived at Fragrant Hills — the Beijing autumn that everyone talks about. This imperial park at the foot of the Western Mountains has been a retreat since the Jin dynasty, eight hundred years ago — emperors built temples here, and the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors made it a summer escape of palaces and pines. The park's name comes from the hill's twin peaks — said to smell of sweet incense, though what draws the crowds is color: every late October into November, the mountainsides of smoke trees turn crimson, and half of Beijing hikes up to walk inside that red. The climb to Incense Burner Peak — five hundred fifty meters, stairs most of the way — rewards you with the whole Beijing plain at your feet. On the way, visit the Temple of Azure Clouds at the park's edge, where the body of Dr. Sun Yat-sen, father of modern China, lay in state in nineteen twenty-five. Arrive early on autumn weekends — the red leaves deserve your sunrise, not your traffic jam.

images.credit: Photo: Charlie fong冯成, Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Incense Burner Peak temple ruins at the summit

spots.name: Beijing Zoo
spots.summary: You've reached the Beijing Zoo — China's oldest zoo, opening in nineteen…
spots.transcript: You've reached the Beijing Zoo — China's oldest zoo, opening in nineteen zero six as an imperial experiment garden, and home to its most beloved ambassadors: the giant pandas. The Panda House is the heart of any visit — watch the bears do what they do best: eating bamboo, up to twelve hours a day, or simply tumbling around like living plush toys. Come in the morning, when they're most active and the crowds are thinnest. But the zoo is more than pandas: over ninety years as a public zoo, it grew into one of the world's largest, with golden monkeys, red pandas, and a lakeside setting that makes it as much park as menagerie. Families could spend half a day here; panda-only pilgrims can be done in two hours. One rule applies everywhere: quiet voices, patient eyes — the stars perform on their own schedule.

images.credit: Photo: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Panda House

spots.name: National Museum of China
spots.summary: On the east side of Tiananmen Square stands the National Museum of…
spots.transcript: On the east side of Tiananmen Square stands the National Museum of China — one of the largest museum buildings on the planet, and by visitor numbers, among the most visited on Earth. It was born in nineteen fifty-nine as one of the "Ten Great Buildings" raised for the tenth anniversary of the People's Republic. Inside: over a million and a half objects spanning five thousand years. Seek out the Houmuwu ding — the heaviest surviving bronze vessel of the ancient world, cast three thousand years ago for a royal mother. From oracle bones to Tang dynastic paintings to the exhibits tracing modern China's own story, this museum narrates the civilization end to end. Entry is free, but reserve ahead and bring your passport. Give it half a day — even a rushed highlight tour takes two hours — and start early, before the school groups arrive.

images.credit: Photo: xiquinhosilva, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the National Museum's colonnade on the square's east side

spots.name: Capital Museum
spots.summary: If the National Museum tells China's story, the Capital Museum tells Beijing's…
spots.transcript: If the National Museum tells China's story, the Capital Museum tells Beijing's — and often, more comfortably. Founded in nineteen eighty-one and reborn in a striking new building in two thousand six — a hall of stone and a bronze-walled drum that nods to ancient Chinese forms — it gathers the city's own treasures: Shang and Zhou bronzes, imperial porcelain, folk crafts, and superb galleries walking you through how a little frontier town called Ji became Dadu, then Peking, then Beijing. The galleries are airy, the lighting kind, and the crowds a fraction of the big names — if the National Museum's queue defeated you, this is the dignified alternative. Look for the old Beijing street-life reconstruction downstairs: shopfronts, cricket cages, and courtyard sounds — old Peking rebuilt in a hallway. An hour and a half covers the highlights; the coin and porcelain rooms reward the slow.

images.credit: Photo: Wikimedia Commons file 'Capital_Museum,China.png' (see file page for author/license)

landmark.name: the Capital Museum's bronze-ribbed main hall

spots.name: Ming City Wall Relics Park
spots.summary: Beside the railway station stands something remarkable: the last living piece of…
spots.transcript: Beside the railway station stands something remarkable: the last living piece of Beijing's medieval city wall. For five centuries, a wall of rammed earth and brick, with gates and towers, enclosed the Ming capital. When the city modernized, nearly all of it came down — but this section survived, and the park before you preserves it as a quiet, climbable ruin. At its east end rises the Corner Tower — a vast two-roofed watchtower from the fourteen hundreds, one of the largest surviving watchtowers of any Chinese city wall — its arrow slits still staring down the tracks where the trains now run. Inside the tower, a small museum shows old Beijing's gates and defenses. In early spring, the plum garden below blooms into the city's favorite flower scene. Walk the wall's grassy base at dusk — Beijing, five hundred years ago and five hundred meters from the subway.

images.credit: Photo: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the southeast Corner Tower

spots.name: White Stupa at Miaoying Temple
spots.summary: Turn the corner of a hutong and meet a mountain of white:…
spots.transcript: Turn the corner of a hutong and meet a mountain of white: the Great White Stupa of Miaoying Temple, the tallest structure in old Beijing for centuries. It was commissioned by Kublai Khan in twelve seventy-one and designed by Araniko, a young Nepalese artist whose work bridged the Himalayas — this Tibetan-style dagoba announced the new Yuan dynasty's capital to the world. Fifty meters of white plaster over a temple you barely see — the stupa dwarfs everything, and the best views come from the hutong alleys around it, where café terraces are built precisely to stare at it. The temple museum inside tells its story; locals pray in its courtyard as they have for seven hundred and fifty years. After renovation it reopened brighter than ever. This neighborhood — Baitasi — is now one of Beijing's calmest design-and-coffee corners. Perfect half hour between the Financial Street towers and the hutongs.

images.credit: Photo: EditQ, CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the great White Dagoba

spots.name: Dongjiaominxiang Legation Quarter
spots.summary: This quiet street of European facades was once the most politically charged…
spots.transcript: This quiet street of European facades was once the most politically charged address in Asia. Dongjiaominxiang — its name began as "Rice Lane" — became the legation quarter where foreign powers set up embassies after the eighteen sixty treaties, then fortified itself into a state-within-a-state after the Boxer Uprising of nineteen hundred: banks, post offices, hospitals, and garrisons behind their own walls, foreign territory threaded through China's capital. The buildings you pass — former bank halls, a French post office, Gothic and classical facades — stayed when the era ended, and today the lane is a peaceful, plane-tree-shaded walk through that strange chapter, minutes from Tiananmen and Qianmen. Photographers love the silence; history readers love the walls. Walk it end to end, then slip south into the hutongs. It's a fifteen-minute stroll — and one of the most surprising streets in the city.

images.credit: Photo: Alfons von Mumm, Public domain · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the former French post office building

spots.name: Simatai Great Wall & Gubei Water Town
spots.summary: For the Great Wall's wilder soul, go to Simatai — the section…
spots.transcript: For the Great Wall's wilder soul, go to Simatai — the section where the wall stops being manicured and starts being myth. Built in the Ming dynasty and left largely as time made it, Simatai climbs steep ridges with crumbling bricks, sheer stairs, and watchtowers with names like the Fairy Maiden Tower perched on stone spires. It's the only section of the Great Wall allowed to open at night — lantern-lit towers glow above a valley of water. At its foot lies Gubei Water Town, a resort rebuilt in northern-village style: canals, stone lanes, hot-spring hotels, and the wall floating overhead in evening light. Come late afternoon: walk the wall as the light turns gold, descend into the water town for dinner, and watch the wall light up above you. It's two hours from the city — the farthest of your wall options, and the most unforgettable.

images.credit: Photo: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Fairy Maiden Tower on the Simatai ridge

spots.name: Juyongguan Pass
spots.summary: Juyongguan is the Great Wall's front door to Beijing — the closest…
spots.transcript: Juyongguan is the Great Wall's front door to Beijing — the closest great mountain pass to the city, guarding the gorge through which every invader and every emperor once traveled. The pass today shows a grand Ming-dynasty fortress rebuilt in gleaming stone: twin gatehouses, looping walls hugging the valley, and the inscription that every visitor photographs — "The First Magnificent Pass Under Heaven." The true treasure is older: inside the fortress stands the Cloud Platform, a white-marble archway from the Yuan dynasty, thirteen forty-five. Walk through its tunnel and look up — the walls and ceiling are covered in thousands of carved Buddhas and inscriptions of sacred texts in six scripts: Chinese, Sanskrit, Tibetan, and more — a fourteenth-century monument to one empire's many languages. It's steeper than Badaling, quieter than Badaling, and under ninety minutes from the city. For a wall trip without the crowds, this is the insider's choice.

images.credit: Photo: Charlie fong, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Cloud Platform with marble carvings

spots.name: Soong Ching-ling's Former Residence
spots.summary: Tucked on the north shore of Shichahai lies one of Beijing's most…
spots.transcript: Tucked on the north shore of Shichahai lies one of Beijing's most graceful hidden gardens — the former garden of Prince Chun's mansion, and for the last decades of her life, the home of Soong Ching-ling. To understand her, hold this in mind: she married Sun Yat-sen, father of modern China, and after his death became a founding figure of the People's Republic — honored as its Honorary President until her death in nineteen eighty-one. She lived here from nineteen sixty-three: a lakeside hall where she worked, entertained, and raised doves — the dovecote still stands. The rooms keep her furniture, her books, her simple desk; the garden keeps the old aristocratic bones — rockeries, ancient trees, water. Few foreign visitors find this place, which is exactly its charm. Pair it with the Drum and Bell Towers nearby, and let the quiet of the garden explain the person better than any plaque.

images.credit: Photo: The original uploader was 用心阁 at Chinese Wikipedia., CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the lakeside main hall of the former Prince Chun's garden

spots.name: Silk Street Market
spots.summary: Silk Street is Beijing's most famous bargaining arena. It began in the…
spots.transcript: Silk Street is Beijing's most famous bargaining arena. It began in the nineteen eighties as an outdoor market of silk sellers along this street — foreigners discovered it, word spread, and the stall vendors eventually moved into a bright eight-floor mall you see today, keeping the old name and the old game. The rule of the house: the first price is an opening move, not a number. Start at a third of it, smile, walk away slowly, and watch the price fall with every step. Silk scarves and tailor-made shirts are the classics; tailors here can measure you and deliver a fitted coat in days. The upper floors drift into electronics and souvenirs — quality varies wildly, so buy what you can judge. No haggling skill needed to enter; it's the best free entertainment in Beijing anyway. Set a budget before you go in. Everyone says that. Everyone ignores it.

images.credit: Photo: 維基小霸王, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Silk Street market's main entrance atrium

spots.name: Hongqiao Pearl Market
spots.summary: Across from the Temple of Heaven's east gate stands an eight-floor building…
spots.transcript: Across from the Temple of Heaven's east gate stands an eight-floor building with a glittering specialty: Hongqiao Market — known worldwide as Beijing's Pearl Market, and called by China's own gem trade "the First House of Pearls in the Capital." Floors three to five are wall-to-wall pearls — freshwater strands from a few dollars, saltwater specimens in velvet cases, plus gold, jade, and silk on the other floors. The truth-in-shopping rules of Beijing markets apply doubly for pearls: trust your eyes, ask for certificates on the big purchases, and know that bargaining is expected from the very first quote. Even if you buy nothing, come at mid-morning when the traders are cheerful and the aisles perform their orchestra of offers. Then walk straight into the Temple of Heaven opposite — prayer first, pearls after — the most Beijing pairing of the sacred and the retail.

images.credit: Photo: AndreyFilippov.com, CC BY 2.0 · via Flickr

landmark.name: the Hongqiao Market building by the Temple of Heaven's east gate

spots.name: Temple of Earth (Ditan Park)
spots.summary: Where heaven got a circle, earth got a square. Ditan, the Temple…
spots.transcript: Where heaven got a circle, earth got a square. Ditan, the Temple of Earth, was built in the fifteen thirties as the counterpart to the Temple of Heaven — and for nearly five centuries, emperors came here each summer solstice to sacrifice to the Earth deity from this stark square stone terrace, the largest of its kind. Today it's a beloved park of old cypresses, and the city's most famous temple fair ground: every Spring Festival, Ditan hosts Beijing's biggest fair — lion dances, folk crafts, snack stalls in a happy crush of locals. The literary-minded know it from a beloved essay, "I and Ditan" by the writer Shi Tiesheng, who spent years in these alleys thinking about fate after illness — the park remembers him fondly. Quiet on ordinary days, roaring at New Year — Ditan is heaven's mirror and Beijing's living room.

images.credit: Photo: Zheng Zhou, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the square altar terrace of the Temple of Earth

spots.name: Ritan Park (Temple of the Sun)
spots.summary: Ritan, the Temple of the Sun, is the smallest and calmest of…
spots.transcript: Ritan, the Temple of the Sun, is the smallest and calmest of Beijing's imperial altars — built in the fifteen thirties, when the Ming court institutionalized worship of sun, moon, earth, and heaven across the city. Each spring equinox, the emperor traveled here to greet the rising sun from the white stone altar that still sits under the cypresses today. Its imperial job long gone, Ritan became one of Beijing's favorite neighborhood parks: a rock garden, a lotus pond, pavilions gifted by sister cities, and at dawn, its legendary community — retirees practicing tai chi, sword dancing, and ballroom steps with total commitment. Business travelers from the nearby embassy district jog here at lunch. If you want to see daily Beijing life at its most graceful, come at seven in the morning: the altar of the sun is now, quite literally, a stage for the people.

images.credit: Photo: ernop, CC BY 2.0 · via Flickr

landmark.name: the sun altar terrace under the cypresses

spots.name: Yuetan Park (Temple of the Moon)
spots.summary: Yuetan is the moon's address in Beijing — the Temple of the…
spots.transcript: Yuetan is the moon's address in Beijing — the Temple of the Moon, built in the fifteen thirties in the same great program of imperial altars that gave the city its Temple of Heaven and Earth. Each autumn equinox, the emperor came here at dusk to sacrifice to the moon as the harvest moon rose. The ritual is gone; the atmosphere remains — and it fits the theme. This is the quietest of Beijing's altar-parks: a deep, green, low-key place of old trees and wide paths, where the city noise fades early and evening light does its best work. Locals come to play chess, practice instruments, and walk off dinner. Astronomy-minded visitors like the symmetry: heaven to the south, earth to the north, sun east, moon west — the altars once mapped the cosmos onto Beijing's map. Stand here at dusk and the design still makes sense.

images.credit: Photo: Dirrival, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the moon altar platform

spots.name: Imperial Ancestral Temple (Taimiao)
spots.summary: Immediately right of the Forbidden City's gate — behind the red wall…
spots.transcript: Immediately right of the Forbidden City's gate — behind the red wall most visitors walk straight past — hides the Imperial Ancestral Temple, Taimiao: where Ming and Qing emperors worshipped their ancestors. Built in fourteen twenty with the palace itself, under the ancient rule that a capital must have "the ancestral temple on the left, the altars of soil and grain on the right." Emperors came here for every coronation, wedding, and victory to report to the imperial dead. Its three great timber halls — the largest cluster of ancient hall architecture outside the palace itself — still stand in a forest of ancient cypresses, some said to be planted by early Ming hands. In nineteen twenty-four it became the Working People's Cultural Palace, but the cypresses don't care about names. Come here when the Forbidden City tickets sell out — same red walls, none of the crowds — and walk the avenue of thousand-year-old-looking trees.

images.credit: Photo: Legolas1024, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the great hall's triple roofline among ancient cypresses

spots.name: Zhongshan Park & Altar of Land and Grain
spots.summary: Behind the Forbidden City's other side waits Zhongshan Park — and its…
spots.transcript: Behind the Forbidden City's other side waits Zhongshan Park — and its heart is the strangest altar in Beijing: a square terrace filled with soil of five colors — red, black, white, green, yellow — one for each direction of the empire plus the center. This was the Altar of Land and Grain, built in fourteen twenty-one, where emperors sacrificed for the realm's harvests; the five-colored earth was brought from every province, making this small platform the empire in miniature. When the empire fell, the park renamed itself for Sun Yat-sen — Zhongshan — and opened to the public. Today it's Beijing's most civilized park: cypress alleys, peony beds in late April, pavilion teahouses, and elderly choruses whose repertoire spans revolutionary songs and love ballads. Enter from the Tiananmen side; you'll be inside the walls of imperial Beijing in one minute — and holding the empire's soil in one glance.

images.credit: Photo: EditQ, CC0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the five-colored earth altar

spots.name: White Cloud Temple
spots.summary: White Cloud Temple is the Vatican of Chinese Taoism — the headquarters…
spots.transcript: White Cloud Temple is the Vatican of Chinese Taoism — the headquarters of the Complete Perfection school, and a working monastery since the thirteen hundreds. Its story centers on Qiu Chuji, the Taoist master who crossed deserts and mountains at age seventy-three to counsel Genghis Khan — the khan, impressed, granted him this temple and exemption from taxes. The temple's origins reach back to the Tang dynasty, though fire and rebuilds keep rewriting its fabric. Inside: halls of the Taoist immortals, the grave shrine of Qiu Chuji, and one beloved ritual — hunt the three stone monkeys carved around the courtyard; locals rub them for luck, and finding all three is said to take a lifetime of visits. At Spring Festival, the temple fair here is Beijing's oldest Taoist celebration. Under the pines, incense smoke and quiet chanting — a completely different Beijing than the palaces next door.

images.credit: Photo: Gene Zhang, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the temple's triple gateway under old pines

spots.name: Dongyue Temple
spots.summary: Across from the CBD's glass towers stands Dongyue Temple — dedicated to…
spots.transcript: Across from the CBD's glass towers stands Dongyue Temple — dedicated to the god of Mount Tai, the emperor of all China's sacred peaks, and judge of souls. Founded in the Yuan dynasty, completed in the thirteen twenties, its fame is a strange and wonderful corridor: seventy-six side halls once held hundreds of clay figures showing what happens after death — the seventy-six departments of the underworld, where every sin had its office and every good deed its record. When the figures were destroyed in the twentieth century, the temple's endless written pleadings to the god survived — visitors can read real prayers, complaints, and thank-you notes from centuries past. Now the Beijing Folk Museum, the temple still bustles with worshippers at New Year, and its stone tablets — more than a hundred — crowd the courtyards like a stone library. Hell has never been so interesting, or so well documented.

images.credit: Photo: G41rn8, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Temple of the God of Mount Tai's entrance screen wall

spots.name: Big Bell Temple (Great Bell Museum)
spots.summary: On Beijing's north side hangs the largest bronze bell in China —…
spots.transcript: On Beijing's north side hangs the largest bronze bell in China — some say the king of all bells. The Yongle Great Bell, cast around fourteen twenty under the Ming emperor Yongle, weighs some forty-six tonnes, stands nearly six meters tall, and carries a hidden miracle: its inner and outer surfaces are engraved with Buddhist sutras — over two hundred twenty thousand characters, said to be flawless in calligraphy. Scientists still marvel at how fifteenth-century foundries cast it in one piece. Struck, it rings for minutes, a sound once heard across the old city; today it sounds only on New Year's Eve, one hundred and eight chimes to end the year. The temple around it, from the Yongzheng era, now serves as the Ancient Bell Museum — three floors of bells spanning four thousand years of Chinese bronze. Come for the big one; stay to realize bells were an empire's clock, alarm, and anthem at once.

images.credit: Photo: User:Clithering, CC BY-SA 2.5 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Yongle Great Bell hanging in the bell gallery

spots.name: Zhihua Temple
spots.summary: Zhihua Temple is a Ming dynasty time capsule with a soundtrack. It…
spots.transcript: Zhihua Temple is a Ming dynasty time capsule with a soundtrack. It was built in fourteen forty-four by Wang Zhen, the most powerful court eunuch of his age — ostensibly a family temple, built, some said, in defiance of rules that eunuchs should build none. Its roofs wear black glazed tiles — a color rank reserved for special favor — and its halls survive almost untouched, one of the most complete Ming wooden temple complexes in the city. Its greater treasure is heard, not seen: Zhihua Temple's Music, the Beijing "jing music" performed by monk lineages for over five hundred years, passed mouth-to-ear across generations and now listed as national intangible heritage. Short recitals are still played here on selected days — sit in a fifteenth-century hall and hear Ming-dynasty sound. Hutong-quiet, crowd-free, and unforgettable: this is old Beijing's most scholarly secret.

images.credit: Photo: danmairen, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Zhihua Temple's black-glazed roof and main gate

spots.name: Fayuan Temple
spots.summary: Fayuan is the oldest temple in inner Beijing — founded in the…
spots.transcript: Fayuan is the oldest temple in inner Beijing — founded in the Tang dynasty in six forty-five by the emperor Taizong, mourning soldiers lost in a disastrous Korean campaign; it was called the Temple for Comforting the Loyal before gaining its present name, "the Source of Buddhist Law." Over thirteen centuries, it has been a prison, a poetry salon, a seminary — today it houses the Chinese Buddhist Academy, and young monks still study in its courtyards. The temple is loved in spring, when its famous lilacs bloom and poets have gathered under them for centuries; the writer Li Ao's novel about the temple made it famous far beyond Beijing. Statues range from a giant seated Buddha to bronze pieces centuries apart. Hidden in the hutongs near the Muslim quarter, it sees few tourists — come at reading hour, when chanting rolls softly across courtyards of ancient trees, and thirteen hundred years sit very lightly on one small temple.

images.credit: Photo: Shizhao, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Fayuan Temple's main gate and bell tower

spots.name: Wanshou Temple (Beijing Art Museum)
spots.summary: Wanshou Temple, the "Temple of Longevity," sits on the Long River —…
spots.transcript: Wanshou Temple, the "Temple of Longevity," sits on the Long River — the waterway Ming and Qing emperors sailed between the Forbidden City and the Summer Palace. Built in fifteen seventy-seven, it became the imperial rest stop on that voyage: emperors would land here, burn incense, and take tea before continuing upstream to their gardens. That river link left it serene and graceful — pagoda, halls, gardens, and centuries of imperial gifts. Today it houses the Beijing Art Museum, its exhibits rotating through bronzes, paintings, porcelain, and Buddhist art from the city's collections; the courtyard gardens reward slow walkers year-round, and the old stage once rang with opera for imperial birthdays. Its neighborhood, Suzhou Street, ties into the river walk toward the Summer Palace — one quiet hour here, then the water onward: you'd be repeating the emperor's afternoon, at a fraction of the budget.

images.credit: Photo: 姚辰伟, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the temple's riverside gate on the Long River

spots.name: Tanzhe Temple
spots.summary: The saying goes: "First there was Tanzhe Temple; then came Beijing city."…
spots.transcript: The saying goes: "First there was Tanzhe Temple; then came Beijing city." This temple in the Western Hills really is older than the capital — founded in the Jin dynasty, over one thousand seven hundred years ago by tradition — making it the oldest temple in the Beijing region, when this valley was wilderness and the city was yet to exist. Its courtyards climb a wooded hillside: the Hall of Dragons, a pond fed by the old dragon well, and its legends. The star is the Emperor Tree — a ginkgo about a thousand years old — which, tradition says, sprouted a new branch for each new emperor's accession. Empress Dowager Cixi came here; poets came here; now you come here — about an hour from the city, best in autumn when the valley turns gold and the temple smells of pine and incense. The mountain walk beyond is easy and lovely. Beijing's oldest resident has earned your half day.

images.credit: Photo: Yumeto, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the ancient ginkgo known as the Emperor Tree

spots.name: Jietai Temple
spots.summary: Jietai, the Ordination Temple, holds one of Chinese Buddhism's most solemn objects:…
spots.transcript: Jietai, the Ordination Temple, holds one of Chinese Buddhism's most solemn objects: its great ordination altar — a marble platform where, for over a thousand years, monks and nuns took their full vows. Tradition ranks it among the three greatest ordination platforms in China — and the temple that holds it, founded in the Tang dynasty in the seven hundreds, was long the licensing authority of the northern Buddhist world: no proper monk north of the Yangtze, the saying went, without Jietai's certificate. The temple sits in hillside quiet west of the city, its courtyards famous for ancient pines with names as good as their shapes — the Free Activity Pine, said to sway when a branch is touched anywhere; the Pine That Embraces the Pagoda, grown around stone. Come in combination with nearby Tanzhe Temple — two ancient temples, one valley, one unhurried afternoon. The incense here burns for discipline, not wishes; you'll feel the difference.

images.credit: Photo: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the great ancient ordination altar

spots.name: Dajue Temple
spots.summary: High in the Western Hills sits Dajue, the Temple of Enlightenment —…
spots.transcript: High in the Western Hills sits Dajue, the Temple of Enlightenment — founded in the Liao dynasty over nine hundred and fifty years ago and loved ever since for its water, its silence, and its flowers. Emperors came here to escape the capital's heat; poets came for the spring. The temple's fame is botanical: its magnolias — planted, tradition says, in the Qing dynasty — bloom each April into the most famous white blossoms in Beijing, drawing crowds for a festival that is essentially perfume and awe. Its clear spring still runs through the garden, feeding the ponds where emperors dabbled; the library hall keeps a Qing-dynasty set of scriptures; the main hall keeps serene Liao-and-Ming-era clay Buddhas. Less than an hour from the city, Dajue makes the perfect half-day: temple in the morning, hillside lunch, and Beijing left far below. Spring for the magnolias; autumn for the ginkgo; winter for having the mountain almost to yourself.

images.credit: Photo: N509FZ, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the temple's clay Buddha hall under the magnolias

spots.name: Temple of Azure Clouds
spots.summary: Climb past Fragrant Hills' gates and you'll find Biyun Temple — the…
spots.transcript: Climb past Fragrant Hills' gates and you'll find Biyun Temple — the Azure Cloud Temple — cascading up the mountainside in six rising terraces, each courtyard promising the next one something better. Founded in the Yuan dynasty era, it grew sumptuous under Ming eunuchs and Qing emperors. Two treasures rule. First: the Hall of Five Hundred Arhats — life-sized clay monks, each with a different face and mood, arranged like a wooden crowd; tradition says your fortune matches the arhat you count to from where you enter. Second: the Diamond Throne Pagoda at the top, an Indian-style stone terrace of the eighteen hundreds with, inside, the memorial to Dr. Sun Yat-sen — his body lay in state here in nineteen twenty-five before burial in Nanjing, and the hall remembers him. Combine with Fragrant Hills for one full mountain day — temple, forest, summit, and history in one climb.

images.credit: Photo: ScareCriterion12, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the Diamond Throne Pagoda on the hillside

spots.name: Wofo Temple (Temple of the Reclining Buddha)
spots.summary: At the foot of the Western Hills, inside Beijing Botanical Garden's grounds,…
spots.transcript: At the foot of the Western Hills, inside Beijing Botanical Garden's grounds, lies Wofo Temple — the Temple of the Reclining Buddha. Its treasure is exactly what the name promises: a bronze Buddha, more than five meters long, lying on one side in the posture of the historical Buddha's final rest — the Nirvana pose — one arm pillowing his head, serenity itself in cast metal. Cast in the Yuan dynasty around thirteen twenty-one, it is among the largest bronze reclining Buddhas in China, and the hall that holds it keeps a dim, hushed atmosphere that fits the subject. The temple began in the Tang dynasty and its gardens — magnolias in spring, wintersweet blooming in the cold of January — make it a four-seasons detour. Combine with the botanical garden's conservatory next door: garden morning, bronze afternoon, and the quietest famous Buddha in Beijing.

images.credit: Photo: Zeus1234, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the great bronze reclining Buddha

spots.name: Yunju Temple
spots.summary: Deep in Fangshan district, southwest of Beijing, Yunju Temple guards one of…
spots.transcript: Deep in Fangshan district, southwest of Beijing, Yunju Temple guards one of the strangest and greatest undertakings in religious history: the stone sutras — Buddhist scriptures carved onto stone slabs, generation after generation, for a thousand years. A monk named Jingwan began the project in the Sui era, fearing the faith's texts would burn as others had; his successors continued until the Ming, carving more than fourteen thousand stone slabs and storing them in mountain vaults and a tower of buried scriptures. The result: the world's largest library carved in stone, sometimes called "the Dunhuang of Beijing." The temple also keeps relics said to include Buddhist sarira. It's two hours from the city — the farthest spot in this guide — but scripture-readers, print-lovers, and pilgrims of persistence call it Beijing's most moving museum. The stones have outlasted ten dynasties. Your train ride will feel brief.

images.credit: Photo: Alexamies, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the stone sutra slabs in the sutra vaults

spots.name: Marco Polo Bridge & Wanping Fortress
spots.summary: The bridge beneath your feet is eight hundred years old — built…
spots.transcript: The bridge beneath your feet is eight hundred years old — built by the Jin dynasty, completed around eleven ninety-two — and famed twice over. First, beauty: Marco Polo described it in wonder, saying no bridge on earth matched it, and so the West named it after him. Its balustrades carry hundreds of stone lions, no two alike — a Chinese tradition says they are too many to count, and visitors have argued the exact number for centuries. Second, history: just beyond its western gate, shots fired on the night of July seventh, nineteen thirty-seven, began the full-scale war between China and Japan — the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, the opening of the Second World War in Asia. The Wanping fortress beside it preserves that night; the Museum of the War of Chinese People's Resistance inside its walls tells the eight years that followed, soberly and powerfully. Walk the bridge at dawn — the lions in morning light, the river valley quiet — and let one small bridge hold both the silk-road wonder and the war that changed the world.

images.credit: Photo: Alanba42, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the stone lions on Lugou Bridge's balustrades

spots.name: Peking Man Site at Zhoukoudian
spots.summary: Fifty kilometers southwest of the capital, a hill called Dragon Bone Hill…
spots.transcript: Fifty kilometers southwest of the capital, a hill called Dragon Bone Hill changed how humanity sees itself. In the nineteen twenties, excavations here unearthed Peking Man — Homo erectus who lived in these caves hundreds of thousands of years ago, used fire, and left the fossil evidence that made one of the twentieth century's great scientific stories. The first complete skullcap was found in nineteen twenty-nine by Pei Wenzhong, after three days of delicate work in the cave mouth before you. Tragically, the original fossils vanished in nineteen forty-one amid wartime chaos — their loss remains one of science's great mysteries — but the site itself, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since nineteen eighty-seven, still yields finds, and the on-site museum rebuilds their world: fire pits, stone tools, and the famous reconstructions. Half a day from the city, best combined with Yunju Temple nearby. Stand at the cave mouth: this is where your morning commute connects to deep time.

images.credit: Photo: Mutt, CC BY-SA 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the excavated cave mouth of Dragon Bone Hill

spots.name: Cuandixia Ancient Village
spots.summary: Ninety kilometers west of Beijing, a whole Ming-and-Qing village sits intact in…
spots.transcript: Ninety kilometers west of Beijing, a whole Ming-and-Qing village sits intact in a mountain fold: Cuandixia, founded centuries ago by a single family — the Han clan — whose descendants still live in its stone courtyards today. The village's name begins with the rarest character in China: 爨, meaning "cooking stove," twenty-nine strokes of homework nightmares and local pride. Built of mountain stone along a hillside shaped — say the feng shui minded — like a gourd or a tablet, its seventy-some courtyards step up the slope in gray stone and black tile, linked by alleys worn smooth by centuries of feet. Filmmakers discovered it long ago; slow travelers followed. Come for a day trip — walk the village spine, climb to the viewing platform for the whole panorama, eat a farmhouse lunch — or stay overnight in a courtyard guesthouse and hear actual silence. It is the Beijing countryside's best-preserved memory, hiding three mountain bends from the highway.

images.credit: Photo: xiaojiecha, CC BY 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the stone village rising up the hillside, seen from the viewing platform

spots.name: Yuan Dadu City Wall Ruins Park
spots.summary: This long, green line across the city's north is a ghost: the…
spots.transcript: This long, green line across the city's north is a ghost: the earthen wall of Kublai Khan's capital. In twelve sixty-seven, the Mongol emperor built Dadu — "the Great Capital" — the planned metropolis that Beijing has been ever since; its walls ran for miles in rammed earth. When later dynasties rebuilt the city smaller, the northern wall was left outside, and centuries of weather softened it into the long hill you can walk today. The park along it stretches for kilometers: cypress walks, bike paths, and a famous spring scene — the Crabapple Blossom Creek, where thousands of crabapple trees flower along a waterway each April and half the city arrives to picnic under them. Look closely at the grassy mounds: this is the thirteenth century, in earth form. Seven hundred years of history, at jogging height — the most accessible ruin in Beijing, and free.

images.credit: Photo: ping lin, CC BY-SA 3.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the earthen wall remnant among the trees

spots.name: Huguang Guild Hall
spots.summary: Off the streets south of Tiananmen hides a perfect wooden opera house…
spots.transcript: Off the streets south of Tiananmen hides a perfect wooden opera house from imperial times: Huguang Guild Hall. Guild halls were hometown clubs for merchants and scholars away from home — this one served merchants from Hubei and Hunan, founded in eighteen oh seven — and its courtyard stage hosted the greatest names of Peking opera's golden age; the acoustics of its all-wood, nail-free structure were part of the show. Today the hall is the Beijing Opera Museum — costumes, scripts, masks, and the stories of the art's two-century rise — and its stage still performs: on scheduled evenings, real Peking opera plays here to a modest, lucky audience. For first-timers, this small hall beats the grand theaters: every seat close, every gesture visible, tea served as it was a century ago. Combine with the nearby Liulichang cultural street for one old-Peking evening. The dynasty is gone; the show, happily, is not.

images.credit: Photo: china_puwa / Alex Yang, CC BY-SA 2.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the opera stage inside Huguang Guild Hall's courtyard

spots.name: Beijing Capital Airport Welcome
spots.summary: Welcome to Beijing Capital International Airport and the start of your visit…
spots.transcript: Welcome to Beijing Capital International Airport and the start of your visit to China's capital. One of the airport's architectural highlights is Terminal Three, designed by Foster + Partners. Its sweeping roof and dragon-like form draw on traditional Chinese colors and symbols — a memorable gateway to the city, whether or not your flight uses this terminal. A few practical words for your arrival: if you are arriving from abroad, have your passport and entry documents ready for immigration. Follow the signs in your terminal for rail connections, official taxi ranks, and other ground transport, and check the current routes and operating hours before choosing your journey. If you need currency exchange or help finding a pickup point, ask at an airport information desk. Beyond the airport, this guide can play stories near listed stops when location and playback conditions allow. Keep the page open and your screen on as you explore. 北京欢迎你 — welcome to Beijing. Your tour starts now.

images.credit: Photo: Simply Aviation, CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: Terminal Three's sweeping dragon-form roof

spots.name: Beijing Daxing Airport Welcome
spots.summary: Welcome to Beijing — and welcome to one of the most spectacular…
spots.transcript: Welcome to Beijing — and welcome to one of the most spectacular buildings humans have ever boarded planes in. This is Beijing Daxing International Airport, opened in twenty nineteen: a single golden terminal spreading six wings like a starfish, designed by the late Zaha Hadid's studio and celebrated as the largest single-terminal airport building on Earth. Follow the signs in your terminal for trains, official taxi ranks, and airport buses, and check the current routes and operating hours before you travel. And if this voice is speaking to you, your guide has begun. From here on, it can play stories near listed stops when location and playback conditions allow — palaces, temples, hutongs, and the wall itself. 北京欢迎你 — welcome to Beijing. Let's begin.

images.credit: Photo: Siyuwj, CC BY 4.0 · via Wikimedia Commons

landmark.name: the starfish-shaped heart of the golden terminal
